rationale: The printed entry's core is directly established by Ezekiel 27's sustained construction of the city Tyre as a single vessel whose boards, mast, oars, pilots, mariners, army, and cargo are its rulers, inhabitants, allies, and commerce; the same figure is reused for Tyre in Isaiah 23 and for Babylon in Revelation 18. Acts 27 and Jonah supply the mechanics of a governed company that can perish while souls are preserved, and the Christ clauses follow from the contrast between walking on the sea and boarding a vessel. No material clause in the entry lacks textual warrant in the cited corpus. The traditional Church reading, while historically prominent for other passages, neither accounts for the Ezekiel definition nor unifies the entry's own reference list as economically.
book_core_identification: An organized kingdom, city, or state riding upon the sea of peoples.
book_secondary_elaborations: Its rulers steer and inhabitants crew it
Christ can rule the waters without a vessel
when He boards one it comes under its true Head
chapter_only_objections: Extended application of the ship figure to Jerusalem/Judea under Caiaphas and to Rome as the larger imperial power
Detailed staging of Mark 4:1 and the parables of the kingdom as preached from a ship-throne
Separation of Noah's tevah from the ordinary ship word while still using the ark as confirmatory structure
Citation of extra-biblical Mediterranean 'ship of state' poets as recognition evidence
strongest_counter_interpretation: The ship most commonly and primarily symbolizes the Church (the barque of Peter / vessel of salvation), with mercantile or political uses treated as secondary, context-bound images of pride or commerce.
counter_core_identification: The Church as the vessel of salvation carrying believers through the world's dangers.
material_core_denial: The counter denies that the primary, definitional referent established by Scripture is any organized kingdom/city/state; it privileges an ecclesial reading drawn mainly from Gospel boat scenes and ark typology over Ezekiel's explicit city-as-ship construction.
counter_case: Patristic and liturgical tradition (nave, barque of Peter) consistently reads the Gospel storm and fishing boats as the Church
1 Peter 3:20-21 and Genesis 6-9 supply an ark-Church typology of salvation through water
Mercantile ships in Ezekiel, Isaiah, and Revelation are merely negative emblems of wealth/pride, not a positive definition of 'ship'
book_explanatory_advantages: Ezekiel 27 literally assembles Tyre plank-by-plank and person-by-person into one ship, then names the wrecked object 'city'
Identical lament language and cargo lists reappear for Babylon in Revelation 18, showing the same political-mercantile referent
Sea-of-peoples versus ship-of-state scale distinction explains why a fish lives in the sea while a ship rides upon it
Christ walking on water versus boarding a vessel supplies a precise contrast that fits the entry's secondary clauses without forcing every boat to be the Church
Acts 27 explicitly distinguishes the perishable ship from the preserved souls aboard
counter_explanatory_advantages: Accounts for the long-standing ecclesial reading of the stilling-of-the-storm and miraculous-catch narratives
Aligns with the architectural term 'nave' and widespread hymnody
decisive_sources: Ezekiel 27:2-36 (city built and wrecked as ship)
Isaiah 23:1-18 (ships of Tarshish / mart of nations)
Jonah 1:4-16 (governed vessel imperiled by one man)
